title: Transport Phenomena in Gases
short_intro: Transport phenomena in gases refer to the net transfer of physical properties such as momentum, heat, and mass due to molecular collisions and thermal motion. These irreversible processes occur when a gas is subjected to gradients of velocity, temperature, or concentration.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of viscosity, thermal conduction, and diffusion in gases, along with their dependence on temperature, pressure, and density based on the kinetic theory of gases.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of coefficients of viscosity, thermal conductivity, and diffusion using mean free path formalism, and analysis of pressure independence of viscosity and thermal conductivity at moderate pressures.

prerequisites: Kinetic theory of gases and Maxwell's distribution of velocities
Concept of mean free path and collision frequency
Degrees of freedom and Law of equipartition of energy

concept_notes.heading: Introduction to Transport Phenomena
bullets: Transport phenomena arise from the molecular transport of momentum, energy, and mass across planes within a non-equilibrium gas.
Molecules crossing a reference plane from regions of different average properties carry their local momentum, energy, or mass into a new region.
These processes lead to the restoration of equilibrium via macroscopic dissipation: viscosity (momentum transport), thermal conduction (energy transport), and diffusion (mass transport).

concept_notes.heading: Coefficient of Viscosity (Momentum Transport)
bullets: Viscosity in gases is caused by the transfer of directed momentum between adjacent layers moving with different velocities.
According to kinetic theory, the coefficient of viscosity η is directly proportional to absolute temperature (√T) and is independent of pressure (or density) over a wide range of moderate pressures.
At very low pressures (when mean free path is comparable to vessel dimensions) and very high pressures, this independence breaks down.

concept_notes.heading: Coefficient of Thermal Conductivity (Energy Transport)
bullets: Thermal conduction in gases is the net transport of kinetic energy of random thermal motion down a temperature gradient.

The coefficient of thermal conductivity K is related to viscosity η and specific heat capacity at constant volume C_v via the relation K = f η C_v, where f is a numerical factor dependent on degrees of freedom.
Like viscosity, thermal conductivity is independent of pressure at moderate densities and increases with absolute temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Coefficient of Diffusion (Mass Transport)
bullets: Diffusion is the transport of mass of a particular chemical species down a concentration gradient.
The coefficient of self-diffusion D is inversely proportional to the density (or pressure) of the gas and directly proportional to T^(3/2).
It describes how gas molecules intermingle due to random thermal agitation and molecular collisions.

derivations.title: Derivation of Coefficient of Viscosity of a Gas
derivations.conditions: Steady state, steady velocity gradient along the z-axis, low density gas where mean free path λ is much smaller than macroscopic dimensions.
steps: Consider a gas with density ρ, mean molecular velocity v̄, and mean free path λ. Let the flow velocity u_x vary along the z-axis such that the velocity gradient is du_x/dz.
Molecules crossing a horizontal plane at z = 0 from a distance equal to the mean free path above (&zbar; = +λ) and below (&zbar; = -λ) transport momentum parallel to the x-axis.
The net viscous drag (force per unit area) F/A across the plane is equated to η (du_x/dz), yielding η = (1/3) ρ λ v̄.

derivations.title: Derivation of Coefficient of Thermal Conductivity
derivations.conditions: Stationary gas with a temperature gradient dT/dz along the z-axis.
steps: Consider layers at distance λ above and below the reference plane z = 0 with temperatures T + λ(dT/dz) and T - λ(dT/dz) respectively.
The net rate of heat energy transport per unit area across the plane is given by Fourier's law of heat conduction: Q/A = -K (dT/dz).

Using the molecular flux and average energy per molecule (Cv T), the thermal conductivity K is derived as K = (1/3) ρ λ v̄ C_v, or in terms of viscosity, K = η C_v (neglecting internal degrees of freedom correction factors).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Viscosity vs Pressure of a Gas
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of viscosity (η) on the y-axis versus pressure (P) on the x-axis, showing a constant horizontal line over a wide range of moderate pressures, dropping off only at very low vacuums.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the surprising kinetic theory result that gas viscosity is independent of pressure because increased molecular density is exactly compensated by a decreased mean free path.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual MCQs asking about the effect of compressing a gas on its viscosity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Viscosity vs Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic-like curve showing viscosity increasing with absolute temperature, typically plotted as η versus T^(1/2).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Reflects that higher temperatures increase molecular thermal speeds v̄, thereby increasing the rate of momentum transfer across layers.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing liquid viscosity (which decreases with temperature) from gas viscosity (which increases with temperature).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell's Determination of Viscosity (Experimental concept)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of oscillating disks or concentric cylinders where an outer rotating cylinder drags an inner suspended cylinder.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to measure gas viscosity by observing the damping of rotational oscillations due to momentum transfer to the surrounding gas.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Understanding experimental verification of kinetic theory transport coefficients.

solved_numericals.question: If the temperature of an ideal gas is increased from 27 °C to 327 °C, by what factor does its coefficient of viscosity change?
solution_steps: Recall the temperature dependence of viscosity: η ∝ \sqrt{T}.
Convert temperatures to Kelvin: T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T_2 = 327 + 273 = 600 K.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the coefficient of thermal conductivity of helium gas at NTP, given that its coefficient of viscosity is 2.0 × 10^-5 kg m^-1 s^-1 and its specific heat at constant volume C_v is 3120 J kg^-1 K^-1.
solution_steps: Use the kinetic theory relation between thermal conductivity and viscosity: K = η C_v.
Substitute the given values: K = (2.0 × 10^-5 kg m^-1 s^-1) × (3120 J kg^-1 K^-1).
Perform the multiplication: K = 6.24 × 10^-2 W m^-1 K^-1.

solved_numericals.question: Explain how the coefficient of self-diffusion D in a gas depends on pressure P and absolute temperature T. Find the combined proportionality.
solution_steps: The diffusion coefficient is given by D = (1/3) λ v̄.
Mean free path λ is inversely proportional to pressure P (or number density n), and average speed v̄ is proportional to \sqrt{T}.
Density ρ is proportional to P/T. Since λ ∝ T/P and v̄ ∝ T^(1/2), combining gives D ∝ \frac{T^{3/2}}{P}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes molecules are hard, elastic spheres with no intermolecular forces of attraction or repulsion (ideal gas approximation).
Assumes the velocity distribution locally follows the Maxwell-Boltzmann equilibrium distribution even in the presence of gradients.
Fails at extremely high pressures where molecular volumes are comparable to total volume, and at extremely low vacuums where mean free path exceeds container dimensions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gas viscosity increases with an increase in pressure because more molecules are packed together.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gas viscosity is independent of pressure over moderate ranges.
common_misconceptions.why: While higher density provides more carriers of momentum, the mean free path decreases proportionally, neutralizing the net effect on transport.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Like liquids, gas viscosity decreases as temperature increases.
common_misconceptions.why: Liquid viscosity is dominated by intermolecular cohesive forces which weaken with heat, whereas gas viscosity is driven by molecular thermal velocity which increases with temperature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Thermal conductivity of a gas depends strongly on the container size.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is independent of container size as long as the mean free path is much smaller than the container dimensions.
common_misconceptions.why: Transport is determined by local collisions within the bulk gas rather than boundary collisions.

quick_revision: Viscosity, thermal conduction, and diffusion are molecular transport phenomena driven by gradients in velocity, temperature, and concentration respectively.
Both viscosity (η) and thermal conductivity (K) are independent of pressure at moderate densities.
Viscosity and thermal conductivity are proportional to \sqrt{T}, whereas self-diffusion varies as T^(3/2) / P.
